questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: The statuses a handler returns for three different requests
questions.learningObjective: trace a request handler to the status it returns
questions.stem: A handler is `function handle(userId, body) { const order = db.find(o => o.id === 9); if (!order) return 404; if (order.customerId !== userId) return 403; if (body && body.items && body.items.length === 0) return 422; return body ? 201 : 200; }` and the order 9 exists and belongs to user 4. Three requests arrive in order: a read by user 4, a create by user 4 sending `{items: []}`, and a read by user 7. Which three statuses go back?

options.text: 200, then 422, then 403, because the checks run in the order they are written
200, then 400, then 403, because a well formed request with nothing in it is malformed
options.misconception: believes a syntactically valid body with no items is a malformed request

options.text: 201, then 422, then 403, because any request carrying a body counts as a creation
options.misconception: believes the presence of a body is what makes a request a creation

options.text: 200, then 404, then 403, because a body that fails a check means the target is missing
options.misconception: believes a failed content check should be reported as a missing resource

questions.explanation: The order of the checks decides the answer, and the order here is the right one: existence, then ownership, then content. The read by the owner has no body and passes everything, so it is 200. The create is well formed and owned but its content is empty, which is a request the server understood and will not act on, and 422 says exactly that. The read by user 7 finds the order and fails on ownership, so 403 rather than 404, which is a deliberate choice about whether to confirm that the order exists. The 404 branch is dead in this scenario, which is itself worth noticing when reading the handler.
questions.hint: Walk the three requests through the checks in the order the function applies them.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: A client that retries one gone status and gives up on another
questions.learningObjective: trace a polling client's behaviour across a run of responses
questions.stem: A client polls a report endpoint with `if (res.status === 404) { retries += 1; } else if (res.status === 410) { giveUp = i; break; } else { done = true; }`, and the responses it receives in order are 404, 404, 410, 404. How many retries does it record, and what does it conclude?

options.text: Two retries, and it gives up on the third response because the resource is permanently gone
Three retries, because the fourth response is also a 404 and the loop never stops
options.misconception: believes a loop that breaks still counts the responses that follow it

options.text: Two retries, and it gives up on the fourth response once all four have arrived
options.misconception: believes the client waits for the whole run before deciding anything

options.text: No retries, because a 404 means the endpoint is wrong rather than the report missing
options.misconception: believes a missing resource is a statement about the address being wrong

questions.explanation: A 404 says this address does not hold that thing right now, which for a report that is still being generated is a normal answer and worth retrying, and a client that keeps retrying it forever is the usual mistake. A 410 says the thing was there and has been removed on purpose, so retrying cannot succeed and the client stops at the third response having recorded two retries. The distinction is the whole reason both statuses exist, and a client that treats them the same either gives up too early on work still in progress or loops forever on work that is finished.
questions.hint: Count the retries as you go and stop at the first response the client treats as final.

questions.topic: What a status-keyed counter records when failures return 200
questions.learningObjective: compute what a dashboard and an alert see when failures return 200
questions.stem: An endpoint returns `res.status(200).json({ ok: false, error: code })` when its write fails, a middleware counts with `metrics['status_' + res.statusCode] += 1`, and an alert fires when the recorded failure rate exceeds half a percent. Over 1,000 requests, 40 of the writes fail. How many failures does the dashboard record, and does the alert fire?

options.text: None of them, and the alert does not fire, because every response was counted as a success
All forty of them, and the alert fires, because the body says the write failed
options.misconception: believes the counter reads the body rather than the status

options.text: None of them, and the alert fires, because forty is more than half a percent of a thousand
options.misconception: believes the alert counts failures the counter never recorded

options.text: All forty of them, and the alert does not fire, because a failure under a 200 is not an error
options.misconception: believes the counter and the alert use different rules on purpose

questions.explanation: The counter keys on the status and nothing else, so a failure that returns 200 is recorded as a success, and the dashboard shows a clean run of 1,000 with an error rate of zero. The alert reads that same zero, so it does not fire even though four percent of what the endpoint actually did was a failed write. This is the reason a failing response must carry a failing status: the body is a description of what happened, while the status is the part every piece of infrastructure reads, and a client that only checks the status is exactly as blind as the dashboard is.
questions.hint: The counter only ever sees the status, so ask what the status was for each of the forty.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: The cost of a chain of redirects to the client
questions.learningObjective: count the requests a redirect chain costs and identify what preserves the body
questions.stem: A client posts a body to `/v1/orders` and is answered with 301 to `/v2/orders`, then 302 to an absolute address, then 307 to the final address, which returns 200. The client's loop is `for (let hop = 0; res.status >= 300 && res.status < 400 && hop < 5; hop++) res = follow(res);`. How many requests does the client make, and which redirect is the one that guarantees the body survives?

options.text: Four requests, and only the 307, because it is the one that keeps the method and the body
Three requests, because the first response is not a request the client makes
options.misconception: believes the original request is not counted among the requests it makes

options.text: Four requests, and all three keep the method, because a redirect only changes the address
options.misconception: believes every redirect status preserves the method and the body

options.text: Four requests, and the 301 is the one, because it is the status the platform recommends
options.misconception: believes the oldest redirect status is the most faithful one

questions.explanation: The loop makes the original request and then follows each of the three redirects, so four requests in total, and the fifth response is the 200 that ends it. What the statuses differ on is the method: a 301 and a 302 have historically been followed by rewriting a post as a get, which drops the body, while 307 and 308 are defined to be followed with the same method and the same body. That is why a body-carrying write should be redirected with 307 or 308, and why a chain of older statuses is a frequent explanation for a create endpoint that mysteriously creates an empty order.
questions.hint: Count the first request as well as the follows, then look for the status defined to preserve the method.

questions.topic: Offset paging and a row inserted above the page
questions.learningObjective: compare offset and cursor paging across a concurrent insert
questions.stem: A table holds ids 101 to 110 in order. A client took page one with `limit=3, offset=0` and saw 101, 102, 103. One row with id 99 is then inserted, and the client asks for page two. Which ids does `offset=5, limit=3` return, and what does a cursor that resumes after 103 return instead?

options.text: 105, 106 and 107, and the cursor returns 104, 105 and 106, so offset skips 104 entirely
104, 105 and 106 either way, because both address the same window of the table
options.misconception: believes the two schemes cannot disagree about which rows come next

options.text: 100, 101 and 102, because the insert shifts every later position by one
options.misconception: believes an insert at the top moves the later rows down rather than up

options.text: 105, 106 and 107, and the cursor returns 106, 107 and 108, because the cursor reads positions
options.misconception: believes a cursor is an offset expressed in a different form

questions.explanation: Offset paging is a count of positions, so the insert pushes every later row one place forward and the window that used to start at 104 now starts at 105. The consequence is the row at 104, which was never on a page the client saw and is now behind the window, so it never appears at all. A cursor records a position in the ordering rather than a number of rows to skip, so resuming after 103 means everything after 103, which is 104, 105 and 106, and the insert does not affect it. This is why a list that changes while it is being read needs a cursor, and why the offset is cheap to implement and expensive to get right.
questions.hint: Work out the list after the insert, then count five positions into it and compare with resuming after 103.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: A store keyed by the idempotency key the client sent
questions.learningObjective: count the effects when repeated requests share a key
questions.stem: A payment endpoint keeps a map and does `if (store.has(key)) return store.get(key); const rec = { id: store.size + 1, amount }; store.set(key, rec); return rec;`. A client sends the same charge three times because the first two responses were lost: two of the requests carry the header value `k1` and the third carries `k2`. How many charges are recorded, and what does the repeated request get back?

options.text: Two charges, and the repeated request gets back the result recorded for its key
Three charges, because every request that arrives is a separate instruction to charge
options.misconception: believes a repeated request cannot be recognised as the same one

options.text: One charge, because the second key is ignored once a key has been seen
options.misconception: believes the store holds a single key rather than one entry per key

options.text: Three charges, because the store only holds results and does not stop the second write
options.misconception: believes recording a key has no effect on what the handler does next

questions.explanation: The store is keyed by whatever the client sent, so the two requests that share a key collapse into one recorded charge and the third, with a different key, is a different charge: two in total. The repeated request does not get refused, which matters more than it looks, because a client that cannot tell a repeat from a rejection has no safe way to retry: it would either pay twice or give up on a payment that had already gone through. The key has to be generated per intended operation rather than per attempt, and the recorded result has to be returned unchanged, or the retry is not doing its job.
questions.hint: Ask how many distinct keys arrive and what the map does with the second one.

questions.topic: Which responses a call filter counts as the server's own
questions.learningObjective: separate caller faults from server faults in a run of responses
questions.stem: A readiness alert runs `responses.filter(s => s >= 500)` over a run of statuses, and its job is to decide whether the service should be paged. For the run 200, 201, 400, 401, 404, 422, 500, 502, 503, 200, which statuses does it count, and how many are there?

options.text: 500, 502 and 503, so three, because the rest describe what the caller did wrong
400, 401, 404 and 422, so four, because a refused request is a service failure too
options.misconception: believes a caller fault is a symptom of the service being broken

options.text: All seven of the non-200 responses, because anything other than success is a failure
options.misconception: believes the distinction between 4xx and 5xx is not worth making

options.text: Only 500, so one, because 502 and 503 describe the network rather than the service
options.misconception: believes a gateway status describes something other than the service itself

questions.explanation: The five hundred range means the server failed to do what was asked: the request was understood and the answer could not be produced, which is what should wake somebody. The four hundred range means the request itself was the problem, whether it was unauthenticated, aimed at something that is not there, or refused on its content, and paging a service because a caller sent a bad token is the alert crying wolf until the real page is ignored. A gateway status is still a failure of the service to answer, so 502 and 503 count, and the run here gives three against four.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: The difference between a safe method and an idempotent one
questions.learningObjective: distinguish safety from idempotence for two methods
questions.stem: A `PUT` on an order replaces the whole order, so calling it twice leaves the same state, and a `GET` never changes anything. How do the two methods differ in the terms the interface uses?

options.text: GET is safe because it changes nothing, and PUT is idempotent because a repeat is the same
GET is idempotent and PUT is safe, because the second is the one that carries a body
options.misconception: believes the two words describe the same property with the methods reversed

options.text: Both are safe, because a request that reports success never changes anything at all
options.misconception: believes every successful request is free of side effects

options.text: GET is unsafe and PUT is not idempotent, because any request with a body can change state
options.misconception: believes a body is proof that a repeat will not land the same way

questions.explanation: The two words answer different questions. Safety is about intent: a safe method is one whose whole point is to read, and a server that honours that will not let a get change anything. Idempotence is about repetition: an idempotent method can be called several times and the effect is the same as calling it once, which is what makes a client or a network free to retry it. A get is both, and a put is idempotent without being safe, and a post is neither, which is why a client that loses the response to a post has a problem a retry cannot solve by itself.
questions.hint: Ask separately what a repeat does and what the method is meant to do.

questions.topic: A version in the path rather than in a header
questions.learningObjective: state what a path version makes visible that a header does not
questions.stem: A client is pinned to one version of an endpoint while the service offers a newer one, and the version is written into the address. What does putting it there buy over writing it in a request header?

options.text: The version is part of the address, so a wrong version is a different resource to everything
A header is stripped on the way through, so a path is the only place a version survives
options.misconception: believes intermediaries remove headers but preserve path segments

options.text: A path can name two versions at once, so a client can compare them in a single request
options.misconception: believes one address can carry two versions for comparison

options.text: A header changes the response rather than the request, so a path cannot carry a version
options.misconception: believes headers act on the answer rather than on the ask

questions.explanation: A version in the path makes the version part of the resource's identity, so a request to the old version and a request to the new one are simply different resources and everything downstream can tell them apart: a log line, a cache key, an access rule, a dashboard of which clients are still on the old one. A version header is equally capable of working, but it is separate from the address, so anything that keys on the address, which is nearly everything, cannot see it. The arguments against paths are about tidiness rather than function, and they are outweighed by being able to answer the question of who is still using the old version.
questions.hint: Ask what a log line or a cache key can tell you when the version is in the address.

questions.topic: One response shape for success and failure
questions.learningObjective: state what a fixed response shape gives a client
questions.stem: An endpoint answers a success with 200 and a body, and a refusal with 400 and a body, and the two bodies are built from the same shape with an error field filled in. What does that arrangement give a client?

options.text: One place to parse and one set of rules to follow, so no outcome is left unhandled
A guarantee that the client never receives a body the endpoint did not describe
options.misconception: believes a shared shape means a shared set of possible values

options.text: A smaller body on a refusal, since only the code is carried and the data is dropped
options.misconception: believes a fixed shape shrinks what a failure has to report

options.text: A guarantee that a failed request still leaves the client holding the previous valid data
options.misconception: believes an error response repairs the client's state for it

questions.explanation: The value is that there is one thing to learn and one place to get it wrong, so a client that has handled one response from this endpoint has handled the shape of all of them, and a new outcome cannot arrive as a surprise the client has no branch for. The error field is what makes it work, because it gives a failure somewhere to go without inventing a second body format. It is worth being clear about what it does not do: a shape cannot make a refusal into a success, and it cannot tell a client whether to retry, which is what the status and any retry advice are for.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: What an integration key and a user token each act for
questions.learningObjective: distinguish what a long key and a short token each authorise
questions.stem: An integration holds a long random key in its server's configuration, and a user's browser holds a short-lived token the service issued to that user. What is each of the two able to authorise?

options.text: The key acts for the integration itself, and the token acts for one user and can be narrowed
The key acts for the user, and the token acts for the whole integration for every caller
options.misconception: believes the longer lived secret is the more specific of the two

options.text: Both act for the user, and the key is simply a token that was never given an expiry
options.misconception: believes a key and a token differ only in how long they last

options.text: The key can be narrowed to single records, and the token can only say yes or no to a call
options.misconception: believes fine grained control is what only a long secret can express

questions.explanation: The two identify different things. A key identifies a caller that is a program rather than a person, it is usually shared by everyone using that integration, and it is revoked by being replaced, so it cannot express much about which person is doing what. A token is issued to a user, carries a claim about who they are, and is normally narrowed to a set of operations and a short lifetime, so it can be thrown away when it leaks. Treating the key as the user's credential is the mistake that produces an integration which can do anything to anybody, because every holder of it is the same caller as far as the service is concerned.
questions.hint: Ask who each credential is standing in for at the far end of the request.

questions.topic: What a token's scope decides
questions.learningObjective: state what a scope limits and who checks it
questions.stem: A service issues one token with the scope `orders:read` and another with `orders:read orders:write` to the same user. What does the scope decide, and who enforces it?

options.text: Which operations that token's holder may perform, checked by the service on each request
Which screens the token may be used from, checked by the browser before the request is sent
options.misconception: believes the scope is enforced by the client that holds the token

options.text: How long the token stays valid, since a narrower scope is issued with a shorter lifetime
options.misconception: believes scope and lifetime are one setting chosen together

options.text: Which fields the response carries, so a narrow scope hides the ones it does not name
options.misconception: believes scope filters the fields returned rather than the operations allowed

questions.explanation: A scope is a statement about what may be done with the token, and it is enforced at the resource server on every request, which is the only place where enforcing it means anything. questions.hint: Ask where a check has to happen for it to be worth anything.

questions.topic: A daily quota beside a per-minute limit
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a quota from a rate limit
questions.stem: A service allows 60 requests a minute and 10,000 requests a day. Which statement describes what the second number is for?

options.text: A total for the whole period, so an allowance cannot be spent in a minute and then be gone
A second speed limit, so a caller over it is slowed down rather than refused outright
options.misconception: believes both numbers express the same kind of limit in different units

options.text: A limit on how many separate callers may reach the service over a day
options.misconception: believes the quota counts callers rather than requests

options.text: A count of failed requests, so a caller is refused once it has failed that many times
options.misconception: believes the day figure counts failures rather than everything

A rate limit is about smoothness: it stops one caller from taking the whole capacity in one burst, and it protects the service and everyone else using it. A quota is about the total: it stops a caller from consuming a day's work in ten minutes, which a per-minute limit allows perfectly happily. A service with only a rate limit can be asked for a million requests spread over a day, so a quota with no rate limit lets a single caller flatten the service in one burst, and the pair together is what makes a shared service survivable.
questions.hint: Ask which question each number answers, and what the other one lets through.

questions.topic: A failure that the client's existing check cannot see

options.text: Rewrite the secret so its characters are encoded in the bundle, so it is not readable there
options.misconception: believes encoding a value in a file the browser downloads hides it from the reader

options.text: About 99.6 percent, so roughly 40 of the 10,000 requests fail
About 99.9 percent, so roughly 10 of the 10,000 requests fail
options.misconception: believes a chain of independent services is as available as its best member

options.text: About 99.6 percent, so roughly 4 of the 10,000 requests fail
options.misconception: believes the four failure rates add up instead of compounding

options.text: About 96.0 percent, so roughly 400 of the 10,000 requests fail

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: A reliability claim the error responses do not support
questions.learningObjective: explain how an interface's own failures can contradict a claim about it
questions.stem: A service is described as fully reliable because it returns 200 on every successful call and has never returned a 5xx. Explain how its own error responses can still contradict that description, and what evidence would settle the question.

answer.exemplar: The claim rests on a status class, and a status class is a summary written by whoever wrote the handler, not a measurement of what happened. A 200 is a sentence the service chose to say, so a service that returns 200 with a body saying the write did not happen has said nothing at all about its reliability, and the absence of a five hundred only establishes that nobody has written that particular sentence. The same gap opens everywhere else: an endpoint that answers 500 for a dependency that is merely slow is counted as a failure the service caused, while an endpoint that answers 200 for a timeout it swallowed is counted as a success it did not deliver, and both distort the number in opposite directions. The evidence that settles it is a definition followed by a measurement. Define the failure first, in terms of what the caller was promised rather than in terms of what the service reported, and then count the responses that break that promise: how many calls returned something the caller could not use, how many were silently degraded, how long each took at the ninety ninth percentile, and what the same measure says about a week rather than a day. Until the definition exists, the two parties are not measuring the same thing, and the disagreement is not a matter of trust.

questions.explanation: A model answer has to say that a status is chosen by the handler rather than measured, give at least one concrete way the service's own reporting flatters it, and conclude that a definition of failure agreed before the measurement is what settles the argument. Merely noting that the dashboard could be wrong misses the point, which is that the two sides are counting different things.
questions.hint: Ask who wrote the status the claim is counting, and what the caller actually received.

questions.topic: The steps of an authorisation code flow
questions.learningObjective: sequence the steps of an authorisation code exchange
questions.stem: Put these five steps in the order they happen in a flow where a browser application is issued an access token for a user, without a client secret.

options.text: The browser sends the user to the authorisation endpoint with the client id and the scope
The authorisation endpoint asks the user to approve and redirects back with a code
options.misconception: believes the code can be sent before the user has approved anything

options.text: The browser holds the code and sends it with a proof key to the token endpoint
options.misconception: believes the code can be exchanged from the address bar alone

options.text: The token endpoint checks the code against the proof key and returns an access token
options.misconception: believes the token is issued before the proof key has been checked

options.text: The browser calls the resource server with the access token attached to the request
options.misconception: believes the access token can be used before it has been issued

questions.explanation: Each step produces what the next one needs, and the arrangement is deliberate in one particular place. The user is sent to the authorisation endpoint first, and the code comes back through a redirect so that it lands in the application's own address space rather than staying in the address bar. The exchange that turns the code into a token then happens over a direct connection from the application to the token endpoint, not through the browser, which is the point of using a code at all: a code that leaked would be useless without the proof key that the application generated and never put in the address. The resource server comes last because there is nothing to present until the token exists.
questions.hint: Ask which step each later one is waiting for, and where the secret is deliberately not needed.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: What rotation does to a copied refresh token
questions.learningObjective: trace a refresh exchange and read what a rejection tells the operator
questions.stem: A service holds one refresh token per user and refuses a presented token that is not the one it holds, issuing the next one in the series on success. User u1 holds `r2`. The holder presents `r2` and receives `r3`; a second copy of `r2` is then presented; afterwards the holder presents `r3`. How many of the three exchanges succeed, and what does the refusal tell the operator?

options.text: Two succeed, and the refusal means a second copy of the token exists somewhere
Three succeed, because a token is still valid until the one it replaced expires
options.misconception: believes an issued token keeps working after it has been replaced

options.text: One succeeds, because presenting a replaced token invalidates the whole series
options.misconception: believes one bad presentation cancels the tokens the holder already holds

options.text: Two succeed, and the refusal is routine, since a client often presents a stale token once
options.misconception: believes a replaced token being presented again is an ordinary event

questions.explanation: Rotation works because each token is good exactly once: r2 becomes r3, so the copy of r2 is spent, and the holder carrying r3 carries on normally, which is two successes out of three. The third exchange is the signal, because a client that only ever holds one token cannot present a spent one unless there are two of them, so the refusal is the detection mechanism rather than a fault. That is also the reason a rotation scheme is worth the extra store: a non-rotating refresh token stays a long-lived credential with no way to notice that it leaked, whereas here the leak announces itself the first time the thief uses it.
questions.hint: Count the presentations of a token that has already been replaced, and ask who else could hold one.

questions.topic: The session cookie a builder assembles from its flags
questions.learningObjective: read the header a cookie builder produces and what its gaps leave open
questions.stem: A builder is `[`${name}=${value}`, `Path=${o.path}`, o.httpOnly && 'HttpOnly', o.secure && 'Secure', `SameSite=${o.sameSite}`].filter(Boolean).join('; ')` and is called as `build('sid', 'abc', { path: '/', httpOnly: true, secure: false, sameSite: 'Lax' })`. What string does it produce, and what is left unprotected by it?

options.text: sid=abc; Path=/; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax, and the cookie can still travel over plain http
sid=abc; Path=/; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax, and nothing about it is left unprotected
options.misconception: believes a flag that was set to false is still written into the header

options.text: sid=abc; Path=/; SameSite=Lax; HttpOnly, and the cookie can still be read by script
options.misconception: believes flag order in the header decides which flags are applied

options.text: sid=abc; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax; Path=/, and the value is written in the clear
options.misconception: believes a cookie value is transmitted without being encoded in the header

questions.explanation: The filter drops any flag whose value is false, so a flag that was not requested is not written, which leaves the header with the path, the restriction on script and the same-site rule. The gap is the missing Secure, which is what would have required the cookie to travel only over an encrypted connection; without it the browser will attach the session to a plain http request to the same host, so anyone on the path can read it. The other three answers all assume the builder produced something other than what its own code does, and it is worth reading the helper rather than assuming which flags a session cookie usually carries.
questions.hint: Work down the array and keep only the parts whose flag is true.

questions.topic: What a scope string actually permits
questions.learningObjective: apply a scope check to four token and requirement pairs
questions.stem: A resource server checks `scopes.split(' ').filter(Boolean).includes(needed)`. Four calls arrive: a token scoped `orders:read` asking for `orders:write`, a token scoped `orders:read orders:write` asking for `orders:write`, a token scoped `orders` asking for `orders:read`, and a token scoped `read:orders orders:write` asking for `orders:read`. Which of the four are allowed?

options.text: Only the second, because a scope has to name the operation in exactly that order
The first, second and fourth, because each of those tokens mentions the word orders
options.misconception: believes a word appearing anywhere in a scope string grants the operation

options.text: The second and third, because a broader scope covers every operation beneath it
options.misconception: believes a general scope implies the specific ones that sit under it

options.text: The first and second, because the requirement is checked for length rather than for name
options.misconception: believes a scope check succeeds when the token holds any scope at all

questions.explanation: A scope string is a set of exact names and the check is set membership, so only the second pair matches: its string contains orders:write as one whole token. The third is refused because orders is not orders:read, and the fourth is refused because read:orders and orders:read are different strings, which is why the vocabulary has to be fixed and documented rather than improvised. The third answer is the one worth guarding against, because a prefix looks like a covering but is only a covering if the service is written to say so, and a service that treats it as a covering has handed every holder of orders:read a way to write.
questions.hint: Split each scope string on spaces and ask whether the needed name is one of the whole words.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: How many times a down store is called by two retrying layers
questions.learningObjective: compute the attempts a retried call chain produces
questions.stem: One client call reaches service A, whose handler is `for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) { try { return callB(); } catch { if (i === 2) throw new Error('A failed'); } }`, and B's handler has the same shape around `callStore()`. The store at the end is down. How many attempts reach the store, and what does that number tell you about retries?

options.text: Nine, because the two retry counts multiply, so a small policy becomes a large one
Six, because the two retry counts add, since each layer can only try once more
options.misconception: believes retries at two layers sum rather than compound

options.text: Three, because only the innermost layer is actually calling the store
options.misconception: believes the outer layer's retries do not reach the dependency

options.text: Nine, but only because the client also retried, so the three layers together did it
options.misconception: believes the number requires a retry at the client as well as at both services

questions.explanation: A's three attempts each become three attempts at B, and each of those reaches the store, so the store sees nine attempts from a single call the client made once. The store is already down, so nine attempts buy nothing at all, and they cost exactly what a struggling service can least afford, because the retries arrive at the moment its connections are already exhausted. This is why a retry policy is only safe in one place in a chain, and why the layer that knows what the caller can tolerate should own it, with the rest either passing the call through or refusing quickly.
questions.hint: Multiply the attempts at each layer rather than adding them, since every attempt nests inside the one above.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: The deadline each service passes to the one below it
questions.learningObjective: compute the deadline a chain propagates to the innermost call
questions.stem: A client allows 3,000 ms for a call. Service A spends 400 ms before calling B and has a limit of 2,000 ms on the call; B spends 300 ms before calling C and has a limit of 1,000 ms; C has a limit of 500 ms. Each service passes down the smaller of the time left and its own limit. What deadline does A pass to B, and what does B pass to C?

options.text: 2,000 ms and then 1,000 ms, because each service caps the time the one below may take
2,600 ms and then 1,700 ms, because the whole budget is passed on and the caps are ignored
options.misconception: believes a service's own limit does not reduce what the one below it is given

options.text: 2,000 ms and then 1,700 ms, because the cap applies once and is not re-applied further down
options.misconception: believes the cap is set at the first hop and inherited unchanged below it

options.text: 3,000 ms and then 3,000 ms, because a fresh budget starts at every hop in the chain
options.misconception: believes each service is given the caller's whole budget for its own work

questions.explanation: A has 2,600 ms left when it calls B, but its own limit is 2,000, so B gets 2,000. B then has 1,700 left against its own 1,000, so C gets 1,000, and C's 500 is the least of the three anyway. Passing the smaller of the remaining time and the service's own limit is what keeps the whole chain inside the caller's budget: a service that passed on all 2,600 would let B take 2,600 and C take 1,700 within it, which is over three seconds for a caller who allowed three, and is why a chain of unpropagated timeouts is a common way to produce a latency that no single service's configuration explains.
questions.hint: At each hop take the smaller of the time left and that service's own limit.

questions.topic: What a breaker lets through over a run of nine calls
questions.learningObjective: trace a breaker's states across a run of calls
questions.stem: A breaker is implemented as `if (state === 'open') return refused; failures = outcome === 'F' ? failures + 1 : 0; if (failures >= 3) state = 'open';`, it opens after three consecutive failures, refuses every call while open, and after the wait admits one trial call whose success closes it again. Over nine calls the dependency fails three times and then succeeds on every call that reaches it. How many calls reached the dependency, how many were refused, and what state was the breaker in at the end?

options.text: Six reached it, three were refused, and the breaker was closed at the end
Nine reached it, because a refused call is still forwarded to be measured
options.misconception: believes the breaker forwards a call in order to discover the dependency has recovered

options.text: Three reached it and six were refused, because the trial call is never allowed to succeed
options.misconception: believes a successful trial leaves the breaker where it was

options.text: Four reached it and five were refused, because the trial is counted as a call that got through
options.misconception: believes a trial call that is admitted does not reach the dependency

questions.explanation: The first three calls fail and the breaker opens, so calls four, five and six are refused without touching the dependency. The trial call is the seventh: it reaches the dependency, succeeds, and closes the breaker, and the last two calls are then passed straight through, which is six reaching it and three refused, with the breaker closed. The point of the whole arrangement is the three refused calls, because a breaker is a way of stopping a service from spending its remaining capacity on calls that are already known to fail, and a breaker that forwards while open has given up the only thing it was for.
questions.hint: Count the calls refused before the trial, then add the trial and everything after it.

questions.topic: The record and the event when a process dies between two writes
questions.learningObjective: count the effects of a crash between a write and a publish
questions.stem: A handler is `db.insert('orders', order); bus.publish('order.placed', order);` and the process is killed between the two lines. How many orders and how many events exist afterwards, and what does the outbox arrangement change?

options.text: One order and no event, while the outbox gives one order and one relayed event
No order and no event, because a killed process rolls back both of its writes
options.misconception: believes a statement that already completed is undone when the process dies

options.text: One order and one event, because the publish is queued before the insert is confirmed
options.misconception: believes a message is sent to the bus before the write that caused it

options.text: Two orders and no event, because the store and the bus are each written once independently
options.misconception: believes two separate stores each record the order for themselves

questions.explanation: The insert completed and the publish never started, so the order exists and the event does not, and nothing in either system will notice: the order is a real row and the event is simply absent. That is the dual write problem, and no ordering of the two lines fixes it, because the failure is between them rather than around them. Writing the event as a row in the same transaction as the order makes the two atomic, so the process can die anywhere and both survive together, and a separate relay then reads the outbox and publishes, retrying until it succeeds, which converts one unwritable pair of systems into one that has already committed and one that catches up.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two statements completed before the process was killed, then apply that to both arrangements.

questions.topic: A client that cannot keep a secret
questions.learningObjective: state why a browser client needs a different flow
questions.stem: An application runs entirely in a browser, so anything it holds can be read by the user it is running for. Which statement describes the flow that fits that situation?

options.text: The browser proves it started the exchange with a value it generated, so no secret is needed
The browser keeps the secret in a script that is only loaded after the user signs in
options.misconception: believes loading a secret later keeps it from the person it was loaded for

options.text: The browser asks the user to type the secret each time, so it never has to store one
options.misconception: believes a credential the user supplies is not a credential the browser holds

options.text: The browser exchanges the code through a page on the authorisation server, so the secret stays there
options.misconception: believes a secret held by the authorisation server protects a client that has none

A stolen code on its own is then useless. The other three do not remove the secret, they only move who has to type it, and the last one changes where the code is redeemed without changing who is redeeming it, which is the part the proof key is there to establish.

questions.topic: What each session cookie flag is for
questions.learningObjective: match the three session cookie flags to the threats they address
questions.stem: A session cookie is set with a path, a lifetime, a restriction on script access, a requirement for an encrypted connection and a same-site rule. Which statement pairs the flags with the threats they reduce?

options.text: Script access allows reading the session, encryption allows sending it, and same-site stops other sites sending it
Script access allows sending the session, encryption allows reading it, and same-site stops its reuse
options.misconception: believes each flag addresses the opposite of what it does

options.text: Path allows reading the session, lifetime allows encrypting it, and same-site allows creating it
options.misconception: believes a scope and a lifetime are forms of protection against disclosure

options.text: Script access allows creating the session, encryption allows scoping it, and path allows ending it
options.misconception: believes each flag controls the lifecycle stage rather than the exposure

questions.explanation: The three address three different routes out. A session that script can read is a session that any injected script can steal, so the restriction on script access is what makes an injection into the page a smaller problem. A session sent without encryption is a session anyone on the path can copy, so requiring encryption protects it in transit. The same-site rule is about who else may cause it to be sent, which is what limits a form on another site from riding the user's session. None of the three protects a session that has already been taken, which is why the value itself is signed and short-lived.
questions.hint: Ask for each flag whether it stops reading, sending, or someone else sending.

questions.topic: What a self contained token cannot take back
questions.learningObjective: state what is lost when the session state is not on the server
questions.stem: A service issues a token that carries the user's identity and expires, and each request is checked by reading the token alone. What can the service no longer do as a result?

options.text: End a session early, because the token stays valid until it expires and nothing can say otherwise
Identify the user, because the identity in the token is only a claim and not a record
options.misconception: believes a token cannot carry an identity at all

options.text: Check the expiry, because a self contained token carries no time of its own
options.misconception: believes an expiry has to be stored on the server to be enforced

options.text: Accept the token twice, because a self contained token can only be used for one request
options.misconception: believes a token is consumed when it is presented

questions.explanation: Checking the token alone means the server holds no session to mark as ended, so the only lever is the expiry, and a token stolen an hour before it expires is good for the rest of that hour. A revocation list or a server side record puts the lookup back for the cases where ending a session early matters more than not looking it up.
questions.hint: Ask what the server would have to change in order to end one user's session before its time.

questions.topic: What a service boundary costs as well as buys
questions.learningObjective: state the coupling a service boundary introduces
questions.stem: An order service is split out of an application so it can be deployed and scaled on its own. What does drawing that boundary introduce?

options.text: A contract between two separately deployable things, so a change on one side can break the other
A copy of the data, so the two sides now have to be told about every change either makes
options.misconception: believes a split duplicates state rather than defining an interface

options.text: A second deployment, so the boundary is mainly a question of how often the two are released
options.misconception: believes the cost of a boundary is the extra pipeline rather than the contract

options.text: A network hop, so the boundary is only ever a question of how long the call takes
options.misconception: believes a boundary matters only for latency

Inside one process a renamed field is a compile error; across a boundary it is a runtime surprise for whichever version happens to be deployed, which is why the contract has to be explicit and why a boundary wants a version of its own. The coupling does not go away when the boundary is drawn, it changes shape: from a reference the compiler checks to an agreement two deployments have to keep.

questions.topic: What a consumer must assume about delivery
questions.learningObjective: state what a consumer must tolerate about duplicate delivery
questions.stem: A consumer reads events from a broker and charges the card each time one arrives. What must the consumer be built to assume about how those events are delivered?

options.text: That the same event can arrive more than once, so each one has to be safe to apply again
That events arrive in the order they were written, so a later one always follows an earlier one
options.misconception: believes the broker preserves the order events were produced in

options.text: That every event produced is delivered, so the handler can assume nothing is lost in transit
options.misconception: believes delivery is guaranteed and only duplication needs handling

options.text: That events arrive only while the consumer is running, so nothing happens while it is stopped
options.misconception: believes a consumer cannot be given anything to catch up on

questions.topic: Separating pools so one caller cannot use them all
questions.learningObjective: state what isolating a pool of workers actually protects
questions.stem: A service gives each external caller its own small pool of workers, with a queue in front of it, and a caller that sends more work than its pool can take is refused. What problem does that arrangement solve?

options.text: One caller cannot occupy every worker, so a slow caller stops being able to starve the others
One caller cannot exceed its own limit, so a shared total is no longer needed anywhere
options.misconception: believes separation removes the need for a limit rather than sharing it out

options.text: One caller's failures cannot be seen by the others, so a single alert covers everything
options.misconception: believes isolation is a way of hiding one caller's errors from the service

options.text: One caller's data cannot be read by another, so the pools also enforce authorisation
options.misconception: believes a worker pool is a security boundary between callers

questions.explanation: The problem is exhaustion. With one shared pool, a caller that sends slow work occupies workers that everyone else needs, and because those workers are blocked rather than busy, the whole service degrades while the offending caller is still being served. Giving each caller its own pool caps how much of the service any one of them can hold, and refusing beyond that is the right answer, because queueing unboundedly only converts a refusal into a timeout that every caller eventually experiences. The pools are not a security boundary and they are not a way of hiding failures, they are a way of bounding the damage one caller can do to everyone else.
questions.hint: Ask what a slow caller does to a pool that every other caller is also waiting on.

Reduce every layer to a single retry, since three attempts per layer is what multiplies

options.text: Add a delay between the retries, so the store has time to come back between them
options.misconception: believes spacing the retries out reduces how many of them arrive

options.text: Retry only on timeouts, so failures that are not timeouts are no longer repeated

Choosing the layer matters as much as the count: the layer that knows what its caller can tolerate should own the retries, and the ones below it should fail fast so the layer above can decide, which is also what makes a slow dependency produce a fast answer rather than a slow one.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: The assumption a call inside the perimeter makes
questions.learningObjective: explain what is given up when an internal call is trusted implicitly
questions.stem: Explain what an internal service call gives up when the caller trusts that the callee is reachable, and what that assumption costs the two of them.

answer.exemplar: The assumption is that because the call never left the building it cannot fail, and it saves real work in the common case: no token, no signature, no permission check on every hop. What it gives up is the ability to tell the difference between two very different situations. When the callee is slow rather than absent, a call with no deadline turns into a caller holding a worker, a request and often a database connection open for as long as the slowness lasts, and the service is up, healthy and answering nothing. Every request queued behind it looks like a slow request, so the symptom appears on the wrong dashboard and the page goes to whoever owns the slow service rather than to the service that is actually stuck. There is also a version of this that never appears in a test: the callee is fine and the network between two things in the same building is the thing that broke, which is exactly the failure the assumption says is impossible. The cost is not that the check is expensive, it is that the shape of the failure becomes invisible while it is happening. What is worth keeping is the trust about identity, which is cheap to establish once for a service identity and is genuinely tedious to do on every hop; what is not worth trusting is reachability, because a deadline and a timeout cost two lines and turn an unbounded hang into an error the caller can act on and report.

questions.explanation: A model answer has to say the assumption makes a hang indistinguishable from a slow success, name the resources the caller holds while it waits, and conclude that identity may be worth trusting while reachability is not. Merely recommending timeouts on everything misses the point, which is that the untrusted call changes where the failure is looked for.
questions.hint: Ask what the caller is holding while it waits, and where the symptom would be reported.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: What a draining process has to finish before it may stop
questions.learningObjective: explain what a graceful drain owes the work already in flight
questions.stem: Explain what a process that is being taken out of rotation still has to do with the requests it has already accepted, and why that obligation is the whole of a graceful drain.

answer.exemplar: A process is stopped in two stages, and the reason for the two is that stopping is not the same as finishing. The first stage takes the process out of rotation, so the thing sending work stops sending it: a load balancer stops choosing the instance, a queue's consumer stops being handed messages, and a scheduler stops adding it as a candidate. Nothing in that first stage touches the work already in hand, and this is the part that has to happen first, because a process that is killed at this point loses every request it had accepted, and the caller has no way to distinguish that from the process never having been chosen. The second stage is the drain: finish what has been accepted, up to a deadline, and only then stop. The deadline is what makes it bounded, and it is the reason a drain is not simply waiting, because a handler waiting on something that will never answer would otherwise hold the process open for ever and turn a routine deployment into an incident. What makes this work is that the two stages are visible to the sender, which is a health or readiness check the process itself reports and the sender respects; a process that keeps accepting work while it drains is not draining, it is just slow, and a process that stops accepting without saying so is being taken out without warning. Where the work is a request the caller is waiting on, the drain's deadline has to be shorter than the caller's patience, or the drain trades one kind of failure for another.

questions.explanation: A model answer has to separate removing the process from stopping it, explain why the requests already accepted are the obligation, and say that the deadline is what bounds the wait. Merely describing a drain as waiting for work to finish misses the ordering, which is that the sender has to stop sending before the drain can mean anything.
questions.hint: Ask what has to happen to the sender before the process may finish what it has started.

questions.stem: A page keeps a count of the requests it has made this minute and stops sending at sixty, and the service has no limit of its own. Which single change makes the limit mean anything?

options.text: Enforce the limit in the service, since only the service sees every caller at once
Move the counter into a service worker, so it survives a page reload before the limit resets
options.misconception: believes the count is unreliable because the page can be reloaded

options.text: Sign the counter so the page cannot reset it, since a reset is what defeats the limit
options.misconception: believes the limit fails because the number is editable by the page

options.text: Obtain a token before counting, so only an authenticated page can spend the allowance
options.misconception: believes a limit is enforceable once the caller is known

questions.explanation: A limit has to be counted where the work is accepted, and the only place every caller passes through is the service. A counter in the page measures the behaviour of one page for one user, and a user who is sent a URL, a script, another tab or a modified copy of the page does not consult it, so the number of requests the service actually receives is unrelated to the number the page believes it made. The other three address ways the page might be circumvented, when the point is that the page is not the thing being protected: the service and everyone else on it are.
questions.hint: Ask where the work is accepted, and who can reach it without the page.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: A chain's availability beside its worst case time
questions.learningObjective: compute a chain's availability and compare its worst case to a budget
questions.stem: A call crosses three services, each independently available 99 percent of the time, and each is bounded by a one second timeout. The caller's own budget is two seconds. First give the availability of the whole chain, then say whether the chain's worst case fits inside the caller's budget.

options.text: About 97.0 percent, and no, because three one second waits make three seconds
About 99.0 percent, and yes, because each hop is inside the budget and so is the chain
options.misconception: believes a chain is as available as one of its hops and as fast as its fastest

options.text: About 97.0 percent, and yes, because the hops run one after another and share the two seconds
options.misconception: believes sequential timeouts share the caller's budget instead of consuming it

options.text: About 99.7 percent, and no, because three timeouts overrun a two second budget
options.misconception: believes the chain's availability is the average of its hops rather than their product

questions.explanation: A request succeeds only if every hop does, so 0.99 cubed is 0.970299, which is about 97.0 percent, and the timeouts do not share the budget: three hops that each wait their full second take three seconds, which is over what the caller allowed. The two numbers are the same design problem seen from two sides, and the interesting conclusion is that a budget of two seconds cannot be spent on three hops of one second each unless each hop knows what is left, which is why the deadline has to be propagated rather than restated at every hop. Shortening the chain fixes both numbers at once.
questions.hint: Multiply the three chances together, then add the three timeouts and compare with the budget.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: A burst tested against a minute limit and a daily quota
questions.learningObjective: apply two limits in turn and count what each one allows
questions.stem: A service allows 60 requests a minute and 1,000 a day. A caller has already made 960 requests today and now sends a burst of 80 at once. First say how many of the burst the minute limit lets through, then say how many of those the daily quota actually allows.

options.text: Sixty through the minute limit, and then only forty through the daily quota
Sixty through the minute limit, and then all sixty, since a day has not passed yet
options.misconception: believes a quota is only applied once the current day is over

options.text: Forty through the minute limit, and then all forty, since the daily figure is the tighter one
options.misconception: believes the daily quota also bounds the rate within a minute

options.text: Eighty through both, since neither limit applies to a caller that is already over the day
options.misconception: believes exceeding a limit suspends the limits for the rest of the period

questions.explanation: The minute limit and the daily quota are two separate gates and both have to be passed, so the burst is cut to sixty by the first and then to forty by the second, because only 40 of the day's 1,000 remain. The twenty requests that pass the minute gate and are then refused by the quota have still consumed rate allowance, which is a detail worth knowing when reading a client's own counters. Keeping the two apart is the point of having both: the first protects the service from a burst and the second stops a caller from spending a day's capacity in a minute and then being useless for the rest of it.
questions.hint: Apply the smaller burst first, then take what is left of the day's allowance.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: Why retrying is only safe for some operations
questions.learningObjective: explain what makes a retry safe and what a client needs when it is not
questions.stem: Explain why a retry is not always a safe response to a failed request, and what a client needs before it can retry the operations where it is not.

answer.exemplar: The asymmetry is that a failure is ambiguous in a way that a success never is. When a request comes back refused, the server is saying it did not do the work, so sending it again is free. When a request times out, the client is saying only that it stopped waiting, and the write may have happened, may be halfway through happening, or may never have arrived; a retry sent as an ordinary new request is a second instruction rather than a repeat of the first. For a read that costs nothing, the first instinct is right. For a create, a payment or a send, it produces the effect twice, and the user is the one who finds out. What makes it safe is something the server can recognise and a key generated once for the intended operation, sent with every attempt, so that the second attempt returns the first attempt's result rather than doing the work again. Where the server cannot do that, the client has to change what it does rather than retry harder: stop and report that the outcome is unknown, show the user something they can reconcile, or make the operation one whose repetition is harmless by designing it to carry an identifier the server stores. The general rule is that a retry is a claim that the earlier attempt did not happen, and the only way to make that claim honestly is to have arranged for it to be checkable.

questions.explanation: A model answer has to say the failure is ambiguous rather than negative, give a case where repeating does harm, and name the key the client generates once as what makes the repeat safe. Merely warning against retries misses the point, which is that the deciding factor is whether repetition has an effect.
questions.hint: Ask what a timeout tells the client about the far side, then ask what the effect of repeating would be.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: The order a table change has to be made in
questions.learningObjective: sequence the stages of a change to a live table
questions.stem: Put these five stages in the order they have to happen in to replace a column on a table that live instances are reading, with no step allowed to break the version that is currently running.

options.text: The new column is added, so both names exist and nothing that reads the old one fails
Code is released that writes both names and still reads the old one, so either version works
Existing rows are filled in from the old name, so the data is present wherever it is read from
Code is released that reads the new name, by which time every row has been filled in
The old column is removed, once nothing reads it and nothing writes it any more

questions.explanation: The order is set by one requirement: at every point, some version of the code is running and every version that can run has to work. Adding the column comes first because it is the only change that cannot break anything. Code that writes both and reads the old one is what makes the backfill safe, since until the old rows are copied a reader of the new name finds nothing, and writing both means a write during the backfill is not lost. Only then is the new name safe to read, and the old one is removed last, once no running instance refers to it, which is why this takes several releases rather than one.
questions.hint: Ask, at each stage, whether the version that is running right now still works.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: The order a consumer makes an event safe to repeat
questions.learningObjective: sequence the steps that make a consumer idempotent
questions.stem: Put these five steps in the order a consumer has to carry them out if the effect of each event is to happen exactly once, even though the event may be delivered more than once.

options.text: The event arrives, carrying the identifier the producer gave it
The consumer checks whether that identifier has already been applied
options.misconception: believes the check can be made before the event has been received

options.text: If it has not, the effect and the record of the identifier are written together
options.misconception: believes the record can be written after the effect in a later step

options.text: The consumer acknowledges, which is what releases the broker to forget the event
options.misconception: believes acknowledging before the work ends is what the broker is waiting for

options.text: The broker delivers the event again, and the check makes the second run change nothing
options.misconception: believes the repeat arrives before the first delivery has been processed

questions.explanation: The two steps that matter are adjacent and have to be in that order. The check has nothing to look at until the event has arrived, and the effect and the record have to be written together, because a consumer that records afterwards has a window in which the same event arrives again, passes the check and is applied a second time. Acknowledging only tells the broker it can move on; the repeat that comes after a restart or a lost acknowledgement is exactly what the check is there for, and it is why the record of what has been applied has to live with the effect rather than in the memory of the process that is handling it.
questions.hint: Ask which two steps must happen as one, and what the consumer has when the event first arrives.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: The order a call is handled when it can fail in several ways
questions.learningObjective: sequence the handling of a call that is bounded, guarded and retried
questions.stem: Put these five steps in the order a service carries them out for one outgoing call that may be refused, may be slow, and may be worth trying again.

options.text: The caller's own budget is recorded, so the rest of the work has something to be measured against
The breaker is consulted, so a call known to be failing is refused without being made
options.misconception: believes the breaker is consulted after the call so that it can learn from it

options.text: A deadline is set as the smaller of the time left and this service's own limit
options.misconception: believes the whole remaining budget is passed on regardless of this service's limit

options.text: The call is made and its result classified as a success, a refusal worth retrying, or a failure
options.misconception: believes the result has to be classified before the call can be made

options.text: A retry happens only if budget remains, and otherwise the failure is reported to the caller
options.misconception: believes a retry is owed to the caller whether or not there is time left for it

questions.explanation: Each step constrains the next. Without a recorded budget there is nothing to compare a deadline against and nothing to decide whether a retry is affordable. The breaker is consulted before the call because its entire value is refusing a call that is already known to fail, and a breaker consulted afterwards has already spent the call it existed to save. The deadline follows, as the smaller of the time left and the service's own limit, so the chain below it cannot overrun this caller's budget. Only then is the call made, and the classification of its result is what decides whether there is a retry, which needs both an error worth retrying and budget left to spend on it.
questions.hint: Ask what each step needs to have been decided before it can be taken.
